### III.2 Stellar Characterization

We use the stellar characterization code uberMS to derive estimates of the physical parameters of the stars from their spectra and photometry. The methodology is described in [37], and further details will be presented in a forthcoming paper, Cargile et al. (in prep). UberMS uses neural networks to interpolate between stellar models, computed using the ATLAS-12 model atmospheres [30] and the SYNTHE radiative transfer code [29]. It simultaneously fits a stellar atmospheric model and corresponding Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) to the input spectrum and photometry. This code functions in two modes. The first mode, called The Payne (TP), fits only stellar atmosphere models and builds on the methods of the stellar characterization code, The Payne [50]. The second mode, called MINESweeper (MS), adds the simultaneous fit of MESA Isochrone and Stellar Tracks (MIST) models updated to include the effects of $\alpha$ -enhancement [13, 36]. This mode builds on the methods of the code MINESweeper [7]. We characterize the stars in this sample using both modes, but default to MS mode (as it utilizes more observational constraints) in our analysis and discussion unless otherwise noted.

We largely followed the methodology of [37] in our implementation of uberMS. The primary differences in our treatment are that we included WISE W1 and W2 photometry, and allowed for higher $A_{\rm v}$ extinction values. For $A_{\rm v}$ , we set a uniform prior from 0.0 to 1.5 times the reddening value as calculated from the [42] dust map in the direction of the target star. We made these changes because our sample includes stars that are farther away, and hence suffer greater dust extinction than those used in [37]. WISE W1 and W2 photometry help to constrain the reddening, particularly when fit simultaneously with the bluer Gaia G, BP, RP magnitudes.

[37] presents benchmarking tests of this stellar characterization method, including comparing the best-fit parameters for an overlapping sample of TRES and the APO Galactic Evolution Experiment 2 [32, APOGEE-2,] targets. We adopt the uncertainties presented in Pass et al. [37] for $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ , $\log g$ , $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ , $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ , and the uncertainties on $R_{\star}$ and $L_{\star}$ from Rodríguez Martínez et al. [40].

[37] prescribes a correction for the best-fit $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ values from uberMS based on the results for Hyades stars of different temperatures. We report both the corrected and un-corrected $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ values. To $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ , we apply the $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ -dependent sixth-order Legendre polynomial correction presented in Table 1 of [37], as determined from fitting uberMS measurement of Hyades stars. We caution that this correction may be metallicity dependent, but it has only been measured specifically at the metallicity of the Hyades. We include here a comparison of the $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ for the 10 targets in our sample that are also found in APOGEE (Figure 2). While we leverage MIST isochrones that account for overall enhancement in $\alpha$ , we expect that our $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ measurements are most sensitive to Mg as that is the dominant $\alpha$ -element with lines in the spectral orders we fit. As such, we compare our $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ to APOGEE’s [Mg/Fe] values. We find good agreement between our $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and corrected $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ values and those reported by APOGEE. There are systematic differences between APOGEE and uberMS at low $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ , consistent with the findings of Pass et al. [37]: APOGEE $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ values extend down to $\sim-0.2$ , whereas the MS values flatten near $0$ . This behavior is reflected in the low- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ outlier in the left-hand panel of Fig. 2. This systematic is not signficant for the findings of this work, however, as it impacts the firmly low- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ thin-disk population.

## IV Data Validation

### IV.1 Stars with Internally Discrepant Results

When assessing the results of our uberMS fits, we considered parameters that are quantitative indicators of poor fits or unreliable results. We discuss those parameters here.

When comparing the $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ as fit using the MS versus TP modes, i.e., with and without isochrones, Pass et al. 37 found an RMS of 51 K. Some stars in our sample displayed a significant disagreement in $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ when comparing these two modes, indicating that the $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ suggested by the spectra and photometry cannot be fit with an isochrone. This can be indicative of an unresolved companion star. We flag the stars in our sample with $\Delta T_{\mathrm{eff}}>100\,\text{K}$ , as they may potentially also be stellar multiples, pending further analysis.

The analysis of some stars resulted in an unusually high spectroscopic line broadening parameter, $v_{\mathrm{star}}$ . This parameter represents line broadening due to both rotational $v$ sin $i$ and macroturbulence. In cases of uberMS fitting high $v_{\mathrm{star}}$ values, either the star truly has a high rotational velocity, in which case we would not be able to estimate precise stellar parameters, or uberMS was attempting to fit two sets of lines, as in a double-lined spectroscopic binary, and compensated by broadening the model spectral lines. In either case, the resulting stellar parameters are not reliable. We remove stars with $v_{\mathrm{star}}>35$ km s-1 from our sample (six candidate planet hosts), and note that $v_{\mathrm{star}}$ may be a useful parameter to consider when vetting planet candidates in the future.

We also examined the “jitter” term (called photjitter), which is added in quadrature to all of the photometric measurement uncertainties used for the SED fitting. In cases where uberMS is not able to find a good fit for the spectrum and SED, especially when forced to respect the parameters imposed by the isochrones, it compensates by increasing the photometric jitter term. We find photjitter to be the most accurate quantitative metric of a qualitatively poor fit to the star’s SED. We removed three additional stars that had both high photjitter and high $\Delta T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ , and as such our stellar characterization results for those three stars were not reliable. We flag our remaining fifteen targets with a photjitter greater than 0.05 mag (a reasonable value given systematic uncertainties between the MIST isochrones and real stars). In most cases, the poor photometric fit manifested in the redder portion of the SED, potentially indicating an otherwise unseen low mass companion or debris disk.

### IV.2 Evolved Stars

Out of our final sample of 268 stars, 52 have $\log g<4.0$ , consistent with significant evolution away from the main sequence. Of these 52, 45 are in the low- $\alpha$ population, 2 are in the high- $\alpha$ population (both have candidate planets) and 5 have ambiguous disk membership. We plot the entire sample on an HR diagram in Figure 3.

Evolved stars lack the “ground-truth” samples that were used to evaluate the accuracy of our measured metallicities for dwarf stars, i.e. for dwarf stars, Pass et al. [37] compared the metallicity measured by uberMS for both members of a binary or members of the Hyades cluster which theoretically have the same metallicity, and the metallicity of asteroid spectra measured by uberMS to solar values. For evolved stars, the uberMS values were only compared to other studies, and Pass et al. [37] found varying agreement. In their comparison to the evolved stars in the Gaia benchmark sample as published in Casamiquela et al. [9], they found good agreement, but found varying offsets in comparison to APOGEE, PASTEL [46] and SPOCS [53]. To account for this, we report larger uncertainties on our best-fit parameters (0.1 dex on $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ , 0.15 on $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ , 0.16 dex on $\log g$ ). We select these uncertainties to match the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) standard deviation found by Pass et al. [37] when comparing MS and APOGEE-determined parameters for the subgiant and giant stars in their sample.

## V Chemical and Kinematic Galactic Disk Classification

### V.1 High- $\alpha$ and Low- $\alpha$ Disk Classification

Using our best-fit $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and best-fit, corrected $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ values for the stars in our sample, we classify each as a member of the high- $\alpha$ disk, low- $\alpha$ disk, or ambiguous. We used the dividing line between high- $\alpha$ and low- $\alpha$ from Weinberg et al. 55, which was determined from the distribution of $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ of evolved stars ( $1<\log g<2$ , $3700\text{K}<T_{\mathrm{eff}}<4600\text{K}$ ) in the APOGEE survey. They define high- $\alpha$ as:

$$ \begin{cases}[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]>0.12-0.13[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}],&[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]<0\\
[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]>0.12,&[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]>0.\end{cases} $$

We identify the majority of our sample as either being in the low- $\alpha$ thin-disk (237 systems) or the high- $\alpha$ thick-disk (5 systems). We identify the remaining 26 systems as having “ambiguous” disk membership. We define this ambiguous population as having metallicities within $\pm 0.04$ dex (our adopted [Fe/H] uncertainty for the dwarf stars in our sample) from the Weinberg et al. 55 dividing line. We note that the lower boundary of the ambiguous population falls just above the bulk of our population, indicating that the ambiguous systems have relatively high $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ within our sample. In the future, more detailed abundance measurements utilizing a broader range of spectral features could be used to sort the ambiguous systems, or one may choose to combine the existing kinematic information with these $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ measurements to classify the ambiguous stars as either thin- or thick-disk. These results are represented in Figures 4 and 5, and in a machine-readable table.

### V.2 Galactic Kinematic Calculations

We calculated a number of kinematic metrics with the goal of classifying these stars as members of the kinematic thin versus thick disks. We used astrometric measurements from Gaia DR3 [22] and an average of the radial velocities measured from the TRES spectra by the standard TRES reduction pipeline [6]. For each star, we first converted the Gaia DR3 parallax to a distance assuming a simple inverse-parallax relation and discarded objects with nonpositive parallaxes. We then constructed astropy.coodinates.SkyCoord objects from the Gaia ras, decs, distances, proper motions, and TRES radial velocities. Using Astropy’s built-in transformation to the Galactocentric frame, we obtained for each star the Galactocentric Cartesian positions and velocities. To express the kinematics relative to the local standard of rest (LSR), we subtracted the solar peculiar motion from Schönrich et al. [43], i.e. $(U_{\odot},V_{\odot},W_{\odot})=(11.1,12.24,7.25)\hbox{\,km\,s${}^{-1}$}$ . We further subtracted a conventional circular velocity at the solar radius of $v_{circ}=220\hbox{\,km\,s${}^{-1}$}$ from the V component. The resulting LSR-frame velocities are represented in the Toomre diagram in Figure 6 and reported in Table 1.

To quantify kinematic thin- and thick-disk membership probabilities, we follow the prescription of Bensby et al. [3], which assumes that the thin disk, thick disk and halo have characteristic velocity dispersions and rotational lags. For a given population (e.g. thin or thick disk) the kinematic likelihood is $f=k\times\exp\left(-\frac{(U_{LSR}-U_{asym})^{2}}{2\sigma_{U}^{2}}-\frac{(V_{LSR}-V_{asym})^{2}}{2\sigma_{V}^{2}}-\frac{W_{LSR}^{2}}{2\sigma_{W}^{2}}\right),$ where $k=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma_{U}\sigma_{V}\sigma_{W}}$ . We adopted the velocity dispersions, asymmetric drifts, local number-density normalizations $X_{i}$ , and thin- and thick-disk densities from Bensby et al. [3] Table A1. Continuing to follow Bensby et al. [3], the relative thick-disk–to–thin-disk membership probability for each star is then $\frac{TD}{D}=\frac{X_{\mathrm{TD}}}{X_{\mathrm{D}}}\,\frac{f_{\mathrm{TD}}}{f_{\mathrm{D}}},$ where $X_{\mathrm{D}}=0.85$ and $X_{\mathrm{TD}}=0.09$ are the adopted local fractions of thin- and thick-disk stars, respectively.

The second metric we used to quantify kinematic thin versus thick disk membership is $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ . We calculated this parameter using the Gala66 6 https://github.com/adrn/gala code [39], which uses the stars’ kinematics to integrate their orbits, determining the maximum height above the Galactic plane that star is expected to reach. In general, a higher $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ is thought to correspond to older, more metal-poor stars [31]. Both the TD/D and $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ of our sample are represented in Figure 7 and reported in Table 1.

### V.3 High- and Low- $\alpha$ versus Kinematic Disk Classifications

In addition to classifying our stars as members of the high- $\alpha$ and low- $\alpha$ disks, we also evaluate their kinematic thick- and thin-disk membership. We represent these kinematic calculations in Figures 6 and 7, and find some disagreement between the chemical and kinematic classifications. We use the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test [54, performed using the scipy.stats.ks_2samp function] to test the null hypothesis that two samples are drawn from the same underlying distribution. We first divide our sample into high- $\alpha$ and low- $\alpha$ disk members (including systems with both candidate and confirmed planets, but discarding the ambiguous-disk systems) and compare their $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ values. This yields a p-value of 0.16, thus not meeting our threshold for significance ( $p=0.05$ ) and not rejecting the hypothesis that the distributions are the same. The same test comparing the TD/D values for the high- $\alpha$ versus low- $\alpha$ disk members yields a $p$ -value of 0.22, similarly representing no evidence to reject that the distributions are the same. These tests suggest that our chemical and kinematic disk classifications do not overlap completely, though this may be due in part to small number statistics. Indeed, if we run the same tests including the ambiguous- $\alpha$ population with the high- $\alpha$ population, we find the two chemically-defined samples now also separate into distinct kinematic components ( $p\leq{0.002}$ ) It is not surprising that including the ambiguous population yields a statistically significant result when excluding them did not, as the high- $\alpha$ thick-disk population is small and therefore does not have much statistical power for the KS test.

We also conduct the same tests in reverse, to check if the kinematically-defined thick-disk members are also chemically distinct. We divide our sample into kinematic thin- and kinematic thick-disk members, first according to their TD/D probability [33, with kinematic thin-disk systems having TD/D $<0.1$ , kinematic thick-disk systems having TD/D $>10$ and systems with values in between being discarded as ambiguous,], then according to their $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ values [56, with kinematic thin-disk systems having $z_{\mathrm{max}}<0.5$ kpc, kinematic thick-disk systems having $z_{\mathrm{max}}>1.0$ kpc and systems with values in between being discarded as ambiguous,]. We then compare the $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ values of these two subsamples. Performing K-S tests, we found evidence that the kinematically-selected thin- and thick-disk subsamples have statistically different $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ distributions, with $p$ -values of $p={0.019}$ when splitting according to TD/D and $p={0.013}$ when splitting on $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ . In general, finding a mixed agreement between the chemically- and kinematically- defined thin and thick disks is not totally surprising, as it is a topic of discussion in the literature [35, 17, e.g.].

### V.4 Validation of Disk Classification Methodology with APOGEE

To get an idea of what kinematics we might expect to see in our chemically-defined samples, we compare them to the kinematics of a random sample of 268 APOGEE stars, matching the size of our scientific sample. We select our APOGEE sample to be within the same $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ , Gaia G mag, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ , $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and parallax ranges as our sample. To minimize halo contamination, we impose that the APOGEE comparison stars have a thick disk/halo probability and a thin disk/halo probability of 10 or greater, in accordance with recommendations from [31]. If we select our comparison sample without considering the $\alpha$ abundances of the APOGEE stars, we find a larger fraction of the comparison sample to be members of the high- $\alpha$ disk than in our science sample. This makes sense, given the correlation between planet occurrence and stellar metallicity. We would expect planet-hosting stars to more often be members of the $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ -rich, low- $\alpha$ sample than the average field star. In order to build a more appropriate comparison sample, we enforce that the APOGEE comparison sample must have the same number of high- $\alpha$ thick disk stars, low- $\alpha$ thin disk stars and chemically ambiguous stars as our science sample.

We followed the same methodology to calculate the APOGEE comparison’s thin versus thick disk membership probabilities and $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ values as we did for our science sample. We show these parameters for the APOGEE comparison sample plotted next to our science sample in Figures 6 and 7. Repeating our tests on the APOGEE comparison sample yields similar results to our science sample. Dividing the sample into high- $\alpha$ and low- $\alpha$ and then comparing their $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ values and their TD/D values both lead to the conclusion that the distributions are likely the same ( $p=0.09$ for $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $p=0.07$ for TD/D). As with the science sample, however, including the ambiguous chemical population in with the thick disk sample leads to the results that the two populations are likely different on the basis of their $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ ( $p=0.003$ ) and TD/D ( $p=0.001$ ). As with the science sample, it seems that the strictly high- $\alpha$ thick disk population may not be large enough to yield a statistically significant KS test result. As with the science sample, splitting the APOGEE comparison sample on their $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ and TD/D values and then comparing their [Mg/Fe] also results in the conclusion that the samples are likely different ( $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ yields $p<0.001$ and TD/D yields $p=0.007$ ).

We find the agreement in the results of these tests between our science sample and this comparison APOGEE sample as confirmation that our science sample results are expected. We again note that such disagreement is precedented in the literature [35, 17, e.g.].

## VI Comparing Hot Jupiter Populations

*Figure 8: Histograms of the parameters of the confirmed planets in the sample. The blue histogram outline represents the low- $\alpha$ population, the solid red bars represent the high- $\alpha$ population, and the hashed red bars represent the high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous populations. The vertical dashed blue line is showing the median of the confirmed low- $\alpha$ planets and the vertical dashed red line is showing the median of the confirmed high- $\alpha$ plus ambiguous planets.*

Given the small sample size of high- $\alpha$ thick-disk systems, we can make only a preliminary analysis of the differences we see between the high- and low- $\alpha$ systems. We present histograms of the confirmed planets’ orbital periods, masses and radii in Figure 8. We also mark the median value for the low- $\alpha$ systems and the median of the combined high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous systems. We detail our statistical comparisons in the Sections VI.1-VI.3.

### VI.1 Comparing Planet Mass

Qualitatively, the masses of the high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous populations appear relatively low in comparison to the low- $\alpha$ population. Comparing the populations via a KS-test does not produce a statistically significant result. Comparing the mass distribution of the low- $\alpha$ systems to the combined high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous systems yields a $p$ -value of 0.07. Comparing only the high- and low- $\alpha$ systems yields $p=0.34$ .

We also approach comparing these populations via a binomial test. Both of our high- $\alpha$ confirmed hot Jupiters (WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b) have masses below that of the median low- $\alpha$ hot Jupiter. We test the probability of drawing two random planets from the low- $\alpha$ population whose masses all fall below the median mass of that population, and find the probability to be 25%. If we consider the high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous populations, the probability of selecting 10/13 planets with masses below the median is 4.3%, which meets a standard 5% criteria for a 2- $\sigma$ difference.

We predict that if the three candidate hot Jupiters hosted by high- $\alpha$ thick-disk stars are confirmed to be true planets and have measured massed $\leq 0.7$ $\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$ , then the difference in high- $\alpha$ thick-disk and low- $\alpha$ thin-disk planet masses would be robustly statistically significant. A KS-test comparing the masses of the strictly high- $\alpha$ and low- $\alpha$ hot Jupiters would yield a p-value of $\leq 0.036$ , and a binomial test would find only a 3% probability of randomly drawing 5 planets from the confirmed low- $\alpha$ population with masses below the median. Such a finding could be evidence that giant planet formation was less efficient in the early galactic environment, resulting in less massive planets. Decreased efficiency could be explained by the lack of Fe and/or $\alpha$ elements resulting in less dense heavy element cores growing more slowly or accreting smaller gas envelopes (because although the high- $\alpha$ thick disk has higher $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ it is still less enriched in total heavy element abundance than the younger, low- $\alpha$ thin disk). It could also be explained by the enhanced radiation in the early galactic formation environment shortening protoplanetary disk lifetimes, reducing the amount of time these giant planets had to accrete gas.

### VI.2 Comparing Orbital Period

Qualitatively, the high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous populations stand out as lacking planets on the shortest orbital periods, with the shortest orbital period among our low- $\alpha$ confirmed planet sample being 1.1 d and the shortest orbital period among either our high- $\alpha$ or ambiguous- $\alpha$ confirmed planet sample being 2.7 d. A KS test does not find a statistically significant difference between the orbital periods of these two populations. Comparing the orbital periods of the high- $\alpha$ confirmed planets versus the low- $\alpha$ confirmed planets yields p=0.87. Including the ambiguous- $\alpha$ confirmed population with the high- $\alpha$ thick-disk population yields p=0.22. A binomial test tells a slightly different story. While the odds of selecting two planets with orbital periods less than 2.7 d from the low- $\alpha$ confirmed population is 60%, selecting 13 planets (the number of high- $\alpha$ systems combined with the number of ambiguous systems) from the low- $\alpha$ population with $P_{\rm orb}>2.7$ d is 3.4%.

Missing high- $\alpha$ hot Jupiters on the shortest orbital periods could be evidence of those planets being destroyed via tidal forces before the system reaches the age of 8 Gyr, but the sample size will need to increase before this finding is robustly statistically significant. We predict that adding three high- $\alpha$ confirmed planets with orbital periods between 2.7 and 10 d to the existing two high- $\alpha$ confirmed planets will yield a statistically significant KS-test result. A statistically significant binomial test result will require the addition of 10 high- $\alpha$ confirmed planets with orbital periods grater than 2.7 d. While ten more high- $\alpha$ confirmed planets would represent a significant increase to the current sample, 2/3 of the high- $\alpha$ candidate planets, all of the chemically-ambiguous confirmed planets and 13/15 of the chemically-ambiguous candidate planets have orbital periods longer than 2.7 d. As such, it is possible that through a combination of confirming existing candidate planets and classifying members of the chemically ambiguous population as high- $\alpha$ thick-disk members, future work could reach this statistically significant population size without needing to add targets to the sample presented in this paper.

### VI.3 Comparing Planet Radius

Qualitatively, the distribution of radius does not appear markedly different between the low- $\alpha$ , ambiguous and high- $\alpha$ populations. Comparing the distribution of radii for the low- $\alpha$ population to either the high- $\alpha$ systems or the combined population of high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous systems with respect to these parameters via a KS-test does not produce a statistically significant result. These tests yield the following: Rp low- $\alpha$ vs high- $\alpha$ (p=0.38); Rp low- $\alpha$ vs high- $\alpha$ and ambiguous (p=0.83).

## VII Notes on Individual Systems

### VII.1 Confirmed Planets Around High- $\alpha$ Stars

Here we will present notes on the two systems with previously confirmed hot Jupiters that we found to orbit members of the high- $\alpha$ thick disk. While thoroughly studied and confirmed as exoplanet systems, they were not previously identified as members of the thick disk. We note that we identify the short-period giant planet currently named in the literature as orbiting a high- $\alpha$ thick disk star, WASP-21 b [4], as belonging to the chemically ambiguous population and discuss it in Section VII.3.1.

#### VII.1.1 WASP-81b

WASP-81 (TOI-5802/TIC 399402994) hosts a hot Jupiter that was first announced by the WASP project in 2017 and studied in detail by Triaud et al. [51]. It orbits a G-type star on a circular, coplanar 2.7 d orbit. It has a radius of $1.43\pm 0.05\,\hbox{$\mathrm{R}_{\rm Jup}$}$ and a mass of $0.73\pm 0.04$ $\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$ . This system has a peculiar architecture, with an eccentric outer brown dwarf companion ( $M\hbox{sin\,$i$}=57\pm 2\,\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$}$ , $P_{\rm orb}=1297\pm 8$ d, $e\approx 0.56$ ). Triaud et al. [51] proposed that if the brown dwarf companion was on its current orbit during the protoplanetary phase then WASP-81 b must have formed in situ, well within the snow line. Alternatively, if the brown dwarf arrived later to the system, WASP-81 b could have already migrated to its current position by the time the brown dwarf entered the system, or the brown dwarf could have driven WASP-81b’s high eccentricity migration.

Our uberMS analysis found WASP-81 to have $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5974\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.27\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.21\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.30\pm 0.09$ . These parameters are consistent with the previously reported parameters, notably the low $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ reported in Triaud et al. 51 of $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.36\pm 0.14$ dex. However, we note that the kinematics of this system are not consistent with the kinematic thick-disk, as its TD/D=0.62 and its $z_{\mathrm{max}}=0.45$ kpc (as stated in Section V, we define kinematic thick-disk systems as having TD/D $>10$ or $z_{\mathrm{max}}>1.0$ kpc).

#### VII.1.2 TOI-5322b

The hot Jupiter orbiting TOI-5322 (TIC 336691874) was confirmed as part of the TESS Grand Unified Hot Jupiter Survey [61]. It also orbits a G-type star on a circular orbit, with $P_{\rm orb}=5.42$ d. It has a radius of $1.48\pm 0.03\,\hbox{$\mathrm{R}_{\rm Jup}$}$ and a mass of $0.58\pm 0.08$ $\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$ . Yee et al. [61] identified TOI-5322 as an old star, with an age of $9.7^{+2.0}_{-1.8}$ Gyr, which is consistent with our finding that it is a member of the thick disk. The age determination from Yee et al. [61] was derived from fitting standard MIST stellar evolutionary models [13, 18] to astrometric and photometric measurements with EXOFASTv2 [19]; we note that one improvement in the present analysis is in the use of $\alpha$ -enhanced MIST models.

Our analysis found TOI-5322 to have $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5809\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.18\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.27\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.15\pm 0.09$ . Yee et al. 61 found this star’s $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ to be $-0.37\pm 0.09$ dex, which is to say more metal poor than we found, but still within a $2\sigma$ agreement. The kinematics of this system are not consistent with the kinematic thick-disk, as its TD/D=0.04 and its $z_{\mathrm{max}}=0.57$ kpc.

### VII.2 Candidate Planets Around High- $\alpha$ Stars

We find three candidate hot Jupiters to be orbiting high- $\alpha$ hosts, TOI-3118.01, TOI-2728.01 and TOI-5781.01. We discuss them here.

#### VII.2.1 TOI-3118.01

TOI-3118 (TIC 58461209) is an early K-type star hosting a $0.93\pm 0.06\,\hbox{$\mathrm{R}_{\rm Jup}$}$ planet on a 3.8 d orbit. Using RVs from Magellan/PFS, we have measured the mass of this planet candidate to be $0.20\pm 0.06$ $\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$ (DiTomasso et al., in prep). We found TOI-3118 to be a subgiant, having a $\log g=3.86\pm 0.16$ , $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5307\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.41\pm 0.10$ dex, and $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.31\pm 0.15$ dex. Because TOI-3118 is an evolved star, its $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ measurement carries an inflated uncertainty, such that within 1 $\sigma$ it is consistent with membership in our defined ambiguous- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ population. An independent measurement of this star’s $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ using Specmatch-Emp [60] on the PFS spectra yields an $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.59\pm 0.10$ dex, agreeing within $1.5\sigma$ and supporting its status as a metal-poor star. An EXOFASTv2 fit, as described for TOI-5322, returns an age of 9.6 Gyr, also in agreement with our understanding of this as an old star. The kinematics of this system are not consistent with the kinematic thick-disk, as its TD/D=0.03 and its $z_{\mathrm{max}}=0.25$ kpc.

#### VII.2.2 TOI-2728.01

TOI-2728 (TIC 42763678) is a $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5714\pm 100$ K star with $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=0.01\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.21\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.17\pm 0.09$ . It displays transit events that would correspond to a $1.38\pm 0.08\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ planet on a 1.7 d orbit. If confirmed, this would be the shortest period high- $\alpha$ hot Jupiter in our sample. Gaia reports a faint companion (3 mag fainter in Gaia G than TOI-2728) 2 arcsec away, which may potentially host the transit detected by TESS. We are currently conducting follow-up observations of TOI-2728 with NEID (2025B-649718, PI: DiTomasso). This star’s $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ meets our criteria for classification into the kinematic thick disk ( $z_{\mathrm{max}}=1.01$ kpc) but its TD/D does not (TD/D=5.65).

#### VII.2.3 TOI-5781.01

TOI-5781 (TIC 279920478) is an evolved star, having a $\log g=3.50\pm 0.16$ , $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5869\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.14\pm 0.10$ dex, and $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.20\pm 0.15$ dex. Owing to its evolved status, TOI-5781’s $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ measurement has a relatively large uncertainty, placing it within 1 $\sigma$ of both our ambiguous- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and low- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ populations. If TOI-5781.01 is confirmed as a planet, more precise $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ measurements, such as from additional $\alpha$ -element lines, will be important to break this ambiguity. It hosts a planet candidate with a radius of $0.9\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ and an orbital period of 5.4 d. The kinematics of this system are not consistent with the kinematic thick-disk, as its TD/D=0.01 and its $z_{\mathrm{max}}=0.24$ kpc.

### VII.3 Select Planets Around Ambiguous- $\alpha$ Stars

We find 26 confirmed and candidate hot Jupiters to be orbiting stars whose $\alpha$ -disk membership we have classified as “ambiguous”. We again note that the entirety of our ambiguous-disk population falls above the majority of the stars in our sample in $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ - $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ space, and are therefore still enriched in $\alpha$ -elements relative to most hot Jupiter host stars in our sample. Here we discuss the four chemically ambiguous systems that meet our criteria for kinematic thick-disk membership: WASP-21b (TOI 5963b / TIC 436478932), TOI-2567b (TIC 258920431), TOI-5594.01 (TIC 53394475) and TOI-3576.01 (TIC 405897415).

#### VII.3.1 WASP-21b

WASP-21 is a G-type star hosting a $1.07\pm 0.06\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ , $0.300\pm 0.001\,\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$}$ planet on a 4.3 d orbit [4]. We found WASP-21 to have $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5946\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.28\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.18\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.32\pm 0.09$ . Both its $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ (1.47 kpc) and TD/D (39) values place it in the kinematic thick disk. Bouchy et al. [4] report the discovery and characterization of WASP-21b, identifying it as the first transiting planet belonging to the thick disk, as determined by its host star abundances. By applying the package Spectroscopy Made Easy [52, SME;] to HARPS spectra, they determine WASP-21’s stellar parameters. They report $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.46\pm 0.11$ and $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.28\pm 0.08$ , which translate to a $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ value of $0.18\pm 0.14$ . Their measured $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ and $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]$ would place WASP-21 directly on our high- versus low- $\alpha$ dividing line, and their reported uncertainties overlap with both our high- and low- $\alpha$ parameter space. In addition to $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{H}]$ and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ , however, they measure ten additional elemental abundances. They argue that because WASP-21’s alpha elemental abundances are approximately twice the value of iron and the other iron peak elements, its abundance patterns in addition to its kinematics and low metallicity support their conclusion that WASP-21 is a member of the thick disk. We agree with this conclusion, and posit that WASP-21 may serve as evidence that, indeed, the chemically ambiguous population that we define in this paper may skew more toward thick- than thin-disk membership.

#### VII.3.2 TOI-2567b

TOI-2567 (TIC 258920431) is a G-type star hosting a $0.97\pm 0.03\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ , $0.20\pm 0.03\,\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$}$ planet on a 6.0 d orbit. We found TOI-2567 to have $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5624\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=0.18\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.10\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.03\pm 0.09$ . This planet was confirmed by Yee et al. 62. They found the $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ of this star to be $0.24\pm 0.09$ , as determined by applying SpecMatch-Synth [38] to HIRES/Keck data, which is in $1\sigma$ agreement with our value. Notably, this star has a $z_{\mathrm{max}}=1.27$ kpc, meeting our criteria for kinematic thick-disk membership. Its TD/D value, however, is 0.5. This indicates that the 3D galactic velocity of this system does not indicate that it is a member of the kinematic thick-disk, but its 6D kinematics do.

#### VII.3.3 TOI-5594.01

TOI-5594.01 (TIC 53394475) is a G-type star hosting a $0.87\pm 0.06\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ planet on a 9.2 d orbit. Using RV measurements from NEID/WIYN, we measure this planet to have a mass of $0.63\pm 0.06\,\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$}$ (DiTomasso et al., in prep). We found TOI-5594 to have $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5871\pm 100$ K, $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=-0.21\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.14\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.13\pm 0.09$ . Notably, it has a TD/D of 50000. We also consider this star’s TD/H, or a ratio of the probability that it belongs to the kinematically-defined thick disk over the halo, and find TD/H=120, placing it firmly in the kinematic thick disk, by this definition. Its $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ value, however, is 0.86 kpc which is significantly larger than the scale height of the thin disk, but does not meet our strict cutoff for thick disk membership. This indicates that, although this star has a high galactic velocity consistent with the kinematic thick disk, its 6D kinematics makes its classification less certain.

#### VII.3.4 TOI-3576.01

TOI-3576 (TIC 405897415) is a $T_{\mathrm{eff}}=5616\pm 100$ K star with $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]=0.01\pm 0.04$ dex, $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]=0.11\pm 0.03$ dex, $\log g=4.28\pm 0.09$ . It displays transit events that would correspond to a $1.16\pm 0.06\,R_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ planet on a 4.6 d orbit. This star’s TD/D meets our criteria for classification into the kinematic thick disk (TD/D=37), but its $z_{\mathrm{max}}$ value does not ( $z_{\mathrm{max}}=0.39$ ).

## VIII Conclusions

We present a homogeneous analysis of 268 confirmed and candidate transiting hot Jupiter hosts, utilizing high-resolution TRES spectra, Gaia, 2MASS, and WISE photometry, and Gaia astrometry to determine key stellar parameters, including $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ . Based on these chemical abundances, we identified two confirmed and three candidate hot Jupiters orbiting members of the high- $\alpha$ thick disk. This work has established the largest sample of chemically-identified high- $\alpha$ thick disk hot Jupiter host stars. These systems are likely ancient, 8 Gyr or older, providing a unique laboratory for improving our understanding of how hot Jupiter formation depends on the galactic environment and how their orbits evolve over extended timescales. The two confirmed high- $\alpha$ systems are WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b; previously determined ages and $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ metallicities for these systems are consistent with their status as old, metal-poor high- $\alpha$ thick disk systems. We also identify 11 confirmed planets and 15 candidate planets as orbiting stars in an ambiguous chemical population. In comparison to literature definitions of the high- $\alpha$ disk and low- $\alpha$ disk, specifically from Weinberg et al. 55, these stars cannot be firmly placed in either population, but they are all relatively high- $\alpha$ in comparison to the bulk of our sample. We highlight two of these ambiguous-disk confirmed planets (WASP-21 b and TOI-2567 b) and two more ambiguous-disk candidate planets (TOI-5594.01 and TOI-3576.01), as their kinematics suggest they are members of the kinematic thick disk.

We note two suggestive findings from our comparison of the confirmed planets in our different disk populations. First, with respect to planet mass, we find both confirmed high- $\alpha$ hot Jupiters and 8/11 of the ambiguous-disk confirmed hot Jupiters to have masses below that of the median low- $\alpha$ planet. Although a KS test does not find a statistically significant difference between the masses of the high- versus low- $\alpha$ confirmed planet population, a binomial test finds it statistically unlikely (4.3% probability) that 10/13 planets randomly drawn from the low- $\alpha$ population would have masses below the median. Confirming the three high- $\alpha$ candidate hot Jupiters and finding their masses to be $<0.7\,\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\rm Jup}$}$ would make this finding robustly statistically significant. Such a mass distinction could indicate that giant planet formation was less efficient in the high- $\alpha$ disk, restricting the mass that could be accreted by these planets at the time of their formation. Planet formation efficiency could have been reduced either by the overall lack of refractory elements [21, despite having higher $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ , the high- $\alpha$ thick disk has a smaller reservoir of $\alpha$ elements in an absolute sense than the younger, low- $\alpha$ thin disk, e.g.] or by the enhanced radiation during their formation period, resulting in smaller giant planets [24]. Alternatively, this could be evidence that the more massive hot Jupiters were destroyed by tidal forces before its system reached its current age of $>8$ Gyr.

Second, we do not find any of our high- $\alpha$ or ambiguous-disk confirmed planets to have $P_{\rm orb}<2.7$ d despite 22% of the low- $\alpha$ population having orbital periods in that range. Again, a binomial test that combines the chemically-ambiguous confirmed planet population with the high- $\alpha$ confirmed planet population finds that there is only a 3.4% chance of drawing 13 planets from the low- $\alpha$ population that all have orbital periods longer than 2.7 d. Increasing the high- $\alpha$ confirmed hot Jupiter population by three, and finding them all to have orbital periods longer than 2.7 d would lead to a statistical difference between the two populations as determined by a KS test. Increasing the high- $\alpha$ confirmed hot Jupiter population by ten would lead to a statistical difference between the high- and low- $\alpha$ population’s orbital periods as determined by a binomial test. This population expansion could arise from: confirming high- $\alpha$ candidate planets that we present here, determining that members of the chemically-ambiguous population we present here are in fact high- $\alpha$ , or expanding the sample. If this conclusion continues to hold with a larger sample, it could be evidence of the shortest period hot Jupiters being destroyed by tidal forces before reaching their current age [25].

While we propose that these differences may be due to varying planet formation processes in high- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ versus low- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ disks, or the result of orbital evolution over gigayear-timescales around the older, high- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ stars, we cannot rule out the possibility that other differences in the underlying stellar populations may be responsible. For example, the difference may be related to the age or evolutionary state of their host stars, e.g. the high- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ host star population consists of a higher fraction of bright main sequence and post-main sequence stars than the low- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ population. Regardless of the origin of the differences, these results showcase that hot Jupiters can persist to these advanced ages, and this population allows us to start testing which factors have influenced this population of ancient, short-period giant planets.

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey (GBTDS) is expected to discover 60,000-200,000 transiting exoplanets, 90-95% of which will be giants, whose host stars will span Galactic populations and chemical abundances [57]. While the majority of these host stars will be too faint and in fields too crowded to be amenable to detailed characterization, this sample will be ideal for building on the questions raised in this work.

Note in review: During the referee process for this manuscript, a relevant work by Ferreira et al. [20] was published, presenting the homogeneous characterization of 32 planetary systems orbiting high- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ and kinematic thick-disk stars. Their sample contained two candidate transiting hot Jupiters, TOI-3277.01/TIC 319568619.01 and TOI-126.01 (note that this was previously reported as WASP-112 b in a preprint by Anderson et al. 1), as well as two previously known hot Jupiters: WASP-183 b (TOI-1927 b) and K2-132 b (TOI-2643 b). These targets are absent from our sample for the following reasons: TOI-3277.01 and TOI-126.01 are too far south to be observed with TRES, WASP-183 has not been observed with TRES, and when characterizing K2-132 via the methods described in this paper, we find its $T_{\mathrm{eff}}<4800$ K and so it is not included in our final sample. Ferreira et al. [20] observed that WASP-183 b and K2-132 b belong to the low-density subset of Jovian planets; this is consistent with our finding that the high- $[\alpha/\mathrm{Fe}]$ planets in our sample have lower masses in comparison to their thin-disk counterparts.

## Abstract

We report the discovery of 10 stars in the Praesepe and Hyades clusters with unusually slow rotation that are likely not field contamination. Even though our search was general, all slow rotators are in the fully convective domain. We find that the fraction of slow rotators in the clusters is more than $5\sigma$ above the distribution expected from field contamination. They provide a potential link between the period distribution of the young open clusters and the field. These stars could be a distinct birth population, or they could be an indication that the onset of strong magnetic breaking is earlier than previously realized in this domain. Photometric variability and X-ray luminosity suggest the later but more data is needed to confirm. Searches for similar populations in younger clusters will help determine when slow rotators first emerge and constrain the timescale and physical mechanisms governing angular-momentum loss in fully convective stars. The discovery of these stars also highlights the importance of long-baseline photometric observations for detecting the long rotation periods of low-mass stars.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

The use of stellar rotation as an age indicator depends on whether stars eventually lose their “memory” of their initial rotation rates; that is, whether their subsequent rotational evolution erases most of the dependence on their initial conditions. Stars are born with a broad distribution of rotation periods, shaped by their initial angular momentum and early star–disk interactions [82, 40, 35, 72]. Magnetic braking subsequently removes angular momentum and causes stars to spin down. Since the torques for rapid rotators are larger than those for slow rotators, convergence in rotation rates at late times naturally occurs. Once this convergence occurs, rotation becomes primarily a function of stellar mass and age, providing the physical basis for gyrochronology [78, 3, 18, e.g.,]. If a subset of stars are born with extremely slow rotation, their weaker spin-down torques will cause them to converge more slowly toward a common rotational sequence, as initially rapid rotators require time to spin down and catch up. These stars can therefore retain substantial memory of their initial conditions, allowing stars of the same mass and age to have very different rotation periods and preventing rotation from providing a unique age.

The predicted convergence of rotation rates is clearly seen in GK stars [22, see for example the data collated in ]. However, the pattern is less clear for the lowest mass stars, where data is sparse in older clusters. Open-cluster studies have revealed a characteristic “waterfall” in the rotation-period distribution near the fully convective boundary: rotation periods increase toward the boundary and then drop abruptly immediately beyond it, accompanied by saturated magnetic activity [36, 60, 13, 14, 72, 15, 32, 39, e.g.,]. Empirically, the angular-momentum distribution of young stars in open clusters appears to evolve more smoothly and monotonically with stellar mass and age than does the corresponding rotation-period distribution [79, 43, 44]. In particular, Kounkel et al. [43] showed that expressing rotation in terms of angular momentum produces a comparatively continuous empirical sequence from FGK through M stars over ages of $\sim$ 10–1000 Myr. This distinction is important because the observed rotation period reflects both the angular momentum of the star and its mass- and age-dependent moment of inertia. Thus, complex structure in the period–mass distribution does not necessarily imply similarly complex underlying angular-momentum evolution.

In contrast to the rapidly rotating M dwarfs observed in open clusters, field-star surveys reveal slow rotators across a broad range of masses [58, 48, e.g.,], including fully convective stars whose inferred ages suggest that slow rotation may be established relatively early in their evolution [64, 49, 9, e.g.,]. However, because ages are difficult to infer for the field stars, the existence of slowly rotators in the field alone does not reveal how rapidly stellar rotation converges toward a common age–rotation relation or how much memory of the initial conditions is retained. Identifying slowly rotating stars in coeval young clusters is therefore crucial for distinguishing between these possibilities and determining when the initial rotation distribution is sufficiently erased for gyrochronology to become a reliable clock.

One significant concern is that young slow rotators may have been missed by previous surveys because of selection effects. FC stars are intrinsically faint, and their long rotation periods (many $>35$ days) require long temporal baselines to measure reliably. Most rotation periods for open clusters have been measured using K2 [29], whose $\sim$ 70-day observing campaigns and broad optical bandpasses limit sensitivity to slowly rotating cool M dwarfs, or TESS [74], whose scattered-light systematics and relatively short observing baselines make rotation periods longer than $\sim 15$ days increasingly difficult to recover [28, 10, 26, 5, e.g.,]. Another reason slow rotators are often discounted in cluster studies is the potential for field-star contamination. Even a small fraction of contaminants can disproportionately populate the slow-rotating tail of a cluster’s observed rotation distribution. Distinguishing genuine cluster slow rotators from field contaminants and observational incompleteness is therefore essential for constraining the true rotational evolution of young stars.

The Zwicky Transient Facility [34, 33, ZTF;] has been observing the northern sky for more than eight years, and its relatively red optical bandpasses make it well suited for measuring the long rotation periods of cool K and M dwarfs. The long temporal baseline is particularly important because the uncertainty of individual photometric measurements can be comparable to the variability amplitude. Repeated sampling of the same rotation cycle can substantially increase the effective signal-to-noise ratio; for example, a 60-day period is sampled over more than 40 cycles across an eight-year baseline. This repeated coverage therefore improves our ability to detect rotation signals in faint, slowly rotating stars. In this paper, we address this missing part of the cluster rotation distribution by searching for long-period rotators in the Hyades and Praesepe using ZTF. We report the discovery of slowly rotating ( $P_{\rm rot}$ $>35$ days) FC stars in both clusters and demonstrate that at least a small population of these stars are consistent with cluster membership rather than being field contaminants. These objects provide cluster counterparts to the slowly rotating fully convective population previously identified in the field, substantially reducing the apparent discrepancy between field and cluster rotation distributions. If confirmed as cluster members, their existence demonstrates that some FC stars can reach rotation periods longer than 35 days by ages $\lesssim 1$ Gyr, either through substantial early angular momentum loss or because some stars are born with relatively slow rotation. In contrast, G- and K-dwarfs are expected to reach rotation periods of $\sim 35$ days only at ages $\gtrsim 8$ Gyr [51].

In section II, we describe the data and rotation-period measurements. In section III, we present the newly identified population of slow rotators. We first investigate whether these stars could be field-star contaminants in subsection III.2. We then examine their rotation-period distributions and magnetic activity properties in subsection III.3 and subsection III.4, respectively. Finally, we discuss the implications of this population for stellar dynamo theory and gyrochronology of fully convective stars in section IV.

## II Data & Method

### II.1 Open cluster membership & existing rotation period catalogs

We chose the Hyades and Praesepe not only because their proximity enables more reliable M-dwarf membership determination and facilitates checks for field contamination, but also because their relatively young ages of $\sim 700$ Myr make them prime targets for searching for young, slowly rotating M dwarfs. In addition, both clusters were observed by K2, providing space-based light curves that can be compared directly with the ground-based ZTF observations. The cluster membership list is taken from [30], in which they applied Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) algorithm to recover cluster members using 5D kinematic information (proper motions, parallax, and Galactic longitudinal and latitude) from Gaia DR3 [19]. A detailed analysis of cluster membership and field contamination is discussed in subsection III.2.

The literature rotation catalogs for the Hyades and Praesepe are taken from [84], which combines rotation catalogs from multiple literature sources based on K2 [29] and Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS; Ricker et al. 74) observations [70, 69, 25, 12, 13, 15, 73, 71, 22, 47].

In addition, we compare the cluster rotation periods with rotation period measurements for field stars. The field-star sample is compiled from several literature sources [54, 75, 48, 50, 5], combining measurements from the main Kepler mission [4], TESS, and the ZTF [34, 33].

### II.2 Light curves & other rotation period catalogs

We perform our analysis using the $r$ -band light curves, which provide the best temporal sampling among the ZTF filters while maintaining greater spot contrast.

We download light curves from Zubercal [16, ZTF Ubercal;]11 1 Available at http://atua.caltech.edu/ZTF/Zubercal.html.. Zubercal is a newly recalibrated photometric data set that improves upon the standard ZTF PSF photometry by simultaneously calibrating all PSF measurements obtained within a given detector quadrant (1/64 of the full field of view) and filter during a single observing night. Compared to the standard IPAC-calibrated ZTF photometry distributed through IRSA, which contains complex systematic photometric residuals of up to $\sim 5$ %, Zubercal removes these systematics and delivers substantially improved photometric precision.

To identify potential failure modes of the Lomb–Scargle (LS) periodogram arising from irregular temporal sampling [86, 17, see also subsection II.3;], we additionally analyzed all available K2 self-flat fielding (K2SFF) light curves downloaded using lightkurve [46] and generated TESS light curves from Full Frame Images (FFIs) using unpopular [27]. The K2SFF light curves [85] correct for the pointing-dependent systematics introduced by spacecraft motion while preserving long-timescale astrophysical variability, while unpopular employs a causal pixel model to remove instrumental systematics while preserving long-period signals. For each of the Zubercal light curves, we bin the observations using a 0.1-day window and remove outliers that deviate by more than 3 $\sigma$ from the main trend. For the K2SFF and TESS light curves, we remove linear trends from each observing season, bin the light curves using a 3-hour window, and remove outliers that deviate by more than 3 $\sigma$ from the main trend. We search for rotation periods with LS periodogram in the range of 0.2-40 days for K2 light curves and 0.2-20 days for TESS light curves, matching close to their observing season length.

In addition, we also compared our measured rotation periods with those reported in large Kepler and TESS rotation-period catalogs [54, 75, 5].

### II.3 Measuring known rotation periods with ZTF

We measured rotation periods in the Zubercal $r$ -band for all stars in the cluster rotation catalogs, regardless of their membership probabilities, to enable a direct comparison with previous studies. Lower-mass stars typically have lower membership probabilities due to larger uncertainties in their Gaia DR3 astrometric measurements, resulting from them being fainter compared to hotter dwarfs. We further discuss and assess the potential impact of field contamination in subsection III.2. This resulted in 886 and 166 stars with measured periods, and 428 and 761 additional stars for which we searched for periods from Zubercal light curves in Praesepe and Hyades, respectively. The color magnitude diagram (CMD) combining the two clusters is shown in Figure 1. The points are colored by their membership probability from [30]. The left panel shows stars with period measurements from various sources (see subsection II.1), while the right panel shows stars without publicly available period measurements.

This does not necessarily indicate that the lower-mass stars are non-members; rather, their fainter magnitudes make it more difficult to distinguish cluster members from field stars based on the available measurements.*

For each star, we downloaded the Zubercal light curve using a 1.2 arcsec search radius and excluded data points with photometric flags or magnitude uncertainties $>0.1$ mag. Most stars excluded due to photometric flags are affected by saturation, for which Zubercal performs poorly at magnitudes brighter than $14$ mag. We only analyzed stars with more than 300 epochs of observations to ensure reliable period measurements. We search for periods between 0.5 and 100 days using the astropy.LombScargle [2, 67, 1] function with Modified Julian Date (MJD), magnitude, and magnitude error as input.

For the initial vetting of rotation periods, we retained only period measurements with a maximum LS power $>0.1$ , a ratio of maximum to median LS power $>10$ (analogous to a signal-to-noise ratio), and a light-curve baseline at least 2.5 times longer than the detected period.

The failure modes of the LS periodogram are primarily caused by uneven temporal sampling, which can produce alias periods, spectral leakage, spurious peaks, and incorrect identification of the true rotation period [86]. The failure-mode periods ( $P_{\rm obs}$ ) produced by uneven temporal sampling can be expressed as a function of the true period ( $P_{\rm true}$ ):

$$ P_{\rm obs}=\left|\frac{m}{P_{\rm true}}+\frac{n}{\delta P}\right|^{-1}, $$

where $m$ and $n$ are integers, and $\delta P$ represents the characteristic sampling period or the period of a systematic signal. To determine the characteristic sampling periods, we compute the LS periodogram of the spectral window function over periods between 0.2 and 1000 days. The spectral window is constructed by assigning unit flux to each observation. We identify peaks that are 3 $\sigma$ above the median LS power, yielding characteristic sampling periods of 0.33, 0.50, 1.00, 363.67, and 444.48 days. We additionally include known periodic systematics, such as the $\sim$ 29.5 day lunar cycle, based on previous studies and empirical inspection of the ensemble period distribution. For vetting, we also excluded any periods that lay within 10% of these known systematics.

Figure 2shows a comparison between the literature periods and the periods recovered from ZTF. The blue points and crosses represent the accepted and rejected periods for Praesepe, respectively, while the orange symbols show the corresponding measurements for the Hyades. The bold crosses indicate ZTF periods that lie on the expected period-alias relations described in Equation 1. We identify these aliases by requiring the observed ZTF frequency, $1/P_{\rm obs}$ , to agree within 10% with an alias frequency predicted from the literature period, $1/P_{\rm true}$ . This approach is possible because the literature periods are independently measured and are not subject to the same uneven-sampling window function as the ZTF observations. The underlying true periods can then be recovered by applying the inverse alias relation. After correcting for these aliases, the final agreement between the literature period catalogs and our ZTF measurements is 93.2% and 95.0% for Praesepe and Hyades, respectively.

For stars with ZTF period measurements deviating more than 10%, which is the typical level of period variation expected from differential rotation [18], from the reported period from the literature, we vetted the K2 and Zubercal light curves and find that most are either missing systematics (see Figure 2, missing aliases that lay close to the alias blue dashed line), or half-period harmonics. For example, Figure 3 shows a case where the K2 and ZTF rotation periods do not agree. This star is particularly interesting because the ZTF light curve exhibits a clear and well-defined peak in the LS power spectrum at a long period of $\sim$ 60 days, while the K2 power spectrum shows a more ambiguous signal. The K2 light curve contains multiple peaks around ( $\sim$ 73) days, close to its observing window, making it difficult to identify the true rotation period. Although some power is present near the literature period, the short seasonal baseline of the K2 observations limits our ability to confidently determine the correct period. In contrast, the long temporal baseline of ZTF enables the detection of longer-period signals. For a 59-day rotation period, the $\sim$ 2000-day ZTF baseline for this star provides approximately 34 rotational cycles in the folded light curve, allowing for a more robust period measurement.

### II.4 Measuring additional rotation periods with ZTF

After testing our period recovery method, we applied the same method to recover periods for stars without reported values in the literature, which include 428 stars in Praesepe and 761 stars in Hyades, of which 219 and 227 stars have more than 300 epochs in Zubercal after restricting to measurements without photometric flags and with magnitude uncertainty $<$ 0.1 mag. Out of these stars, 44 stars in Praesepe and 122 stars in Hyades have maximum LS power $>$ 0.1 and the ratio between the maximum and the median LS power $>$ 10. For these stars, we downloaded and measured periods from the K2SFF and TESS light curves generated from FFIs with unpopular. We also cross-matched our stars with periods from the all sky TESS catalog [5]. For stars with measured periods from TESS, we only keep measurements with maximum LS power $>$ 0.1.

Figure 4shows the comparison between the periods reported by [5] and our period measurements. For stars with a maximum LS power $>0.1$ , our measured periods agree with those from [5] to within 10% for the half-period, quarter-period, and 1:1 period relations. The agreement becomes worse at periods $\gtrsim 10$ days, as expected, since these periods approach the observational baseline of a single TESS observing season. The comparison with previous period measurements serves only as a guideline for assessing the reliability of our detections. We later visually inspect all accepted ZTF period measurements using all available TESS and K2 light curves to ensure the robustness of the identified rotation signals.

### II.5 Photometric variability, binary identification, and $v\sin i$ measurements

For each star, we also measure the photometric variability, $R_{\rm var}$ , by calculating the standard deviation of the median magnitude, $\tilde{m}$ , over the entire light curve. We then convert the variability from magnitudes to relative flux units using $R_{\rm var}=9.21\times 10^{5}\times{\rm std}(\tilde{m})\ {\rm ppm}$ , where the constant factor converts variations in magnitude to relative flux variations under the assumption that the variability is small.

To vet for potential binaries, we first selected stars with re-normalized unit weight error (RUWE) larger than the sky-varying RUWE threshold for binaries determined using the method described in [7]. We also cross-matched our sample and the full cluster sample in [30] with SDSS-V IPL4 APOGEE observations [42, 90, 41] to obtain available radial velocity (RV) and $v\sin i$ measurements. We identified confirmed binaries as stars with multiple good RV measurements from MWM and an RV scatter $>1$ km/s. Based on these criteria, we identify 6 confirmed binaries among the newly measured rotators in Praesepe and 1 in the Hyades.

The difference in period recovery fraction for the Praesepe and Hyades at ( $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ ) $\approx$ 3 could indicate larger field contaimination for the Hyades.

## III Results

In this section, we first validate the long rotation periods with $v\sin i$ measurements in subsection III.1. We then assess the potential impact of field-star contamination in subsection III.2, specifically investigating whether the long rotation periods could be explained solely by contamination from non-member field stars. In subsection III.3, we examine the rotation-period distributions as a function of Gaia $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ color, photometric temperature, and absolute magnitude using the newly measured ZTF periods. We also investigate the activity–rotation relation in subsection III.4. Finally, in section IV, we discuss the implications of discovering these slowly rotating M dwarfs in open clusters younger than 1 Gyr. We explore the consequences for stellar dynamo theory and examine how the existence of such slow rotators may impact gyrochronology models and age determinations for FC stars.

### III.1 $v\sin i$ measurements of the slow-rotators

Because line broadening limits the precision of low $v\sin i$ measurements, values below $\sim 10$ km s-1 for slowly rotating stars are not expected to correlate strongly with rotation period [21, 77, e.g.,]. We therefore compared our measured rotation periods with SDSS-V $v\sin i$ measurements to verify that the candidate slow rotators do not show anomalously large projected rotational velocities. However, it is worth noting that most of the stars with newly measured rotation periods in our sample are K and M dwarfs, for which $v\sin i$ measurements may be artificially inflated to compensate for inadequately modeled spectral lines. We therefore regard the $v\sin i$ measurements as supporting evidence for the slow rotation of these stars, while noting that they should not be treated as an independent, quantitative constraint on their rotation periods.

Figure 6shows the comparison for both clusters, with stars with literature rotation periods shown as crosses and stars with newly measured rotation periods shown as circles. All stars are colored by their $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ color. Higher-mass stars (smaller $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ ) exhibit a stronger and tighter $v\sin i$ - $P_{\rm rot}$ relation than lower-mass stars (larger $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ ), as expected, likely because $v\sin i$ measurements for lower-mass stars can be artificially inflated to compensate for inadequately modeled spectral lines. Our newly measured rotation periods follow a similar declining trend in $v\sin i$ with increasing $P_{\rm rot}$ , and are consistent with stars of similar $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ color with rotation periods from the literature. Stars with rotation periods $>35$ days appear to deviate from the trend, likely because the literature sample contains few stars in this period regime. Nevertheless, all of these stars have $v\sin i$ measurements $<10$ km s-1, consistent with the expected low projected rotational velocities of slowly rotating stars and the measurement limit of $v\sin i$ . This floor is particularly evident for stars with $P_{\rm rot}$ $>10$ days and $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ $>2.5$ , for which $v\sin i$ measurements cluster near the detection limit.

### III.2 Field contamination

One important question is whether these slowly rotating stars could instead be field-star contaminants. In this section, we demonstrate that this concern is valid for some of our longest rotation period stars. However, we do find a significant sample of stars where the background hypothesis is extraordinarily unlikely. To investigate this, we first use the 6D kinematic information from Gaia DR3 and SDSS-V. None of the slow rotators show significant deviations in their 5D kinematics (excluding RV) from the rest of the cluster sample, as expected given that they were identified using 5D kinematic membership information. For the stars with RV measurements, we likewise find no significant kinematic deviations between the slow rotators and the rest of the Hyades sample. We do not have RV measurements for the slow rotators in Praesepe as these stars are too faint for reliable spectroscopic measurements.

We further estimated the probability of field contamination, $P_{\rm field}$ , for each cluster member using Gaussian mixture models to separately model the cluster and field populations in astrometric and photometric parameter space. For each star with observed properties $\mathbf{x}$ (in this case, 5D or 6D kinematics and Gaia $G$ and $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ ), the probability of being a field star is given by Bayes’ theorem,

$$ P_{\rm field}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{p(\mathbf{x}\mid{\rm field})P({\rm field})}{p(\mathbf{x}\mid{\rm field})P({\rm field})+p(\mathbf{x}\mid{\rm cluster})P({\rm cluster})}, $$

where $p(\mathbf{x}\mid{\rm field})$ and $p(\mathbf{x}\mid{\rm cluster})$ are the likelihoods of the star’s observed properties under the field and cluster Gaussian mixture models, respectively, and $P({\rm field})$ and $P({\rm cluster})$ are the adopted prior probabilities. We estimate the prior cluster and field fractions from the membership probabilities of the candidate sample and the total number of field sample with similar 5D kinematics ( $N_{\rm f,5D}$ ). Specifically, the sum of the membership probabilities, $\sum_{i}P_{{\rm mem},i}$ , gives the expected number of cluster members ( $N_{\rm cluster}$ ), while $\sum_{i}(1-P_{{\rm mem},i})$ gives the expected number of field contaminants in the cluster sample. $N_{\rm field}$ is then $\sum_{i}(1-P_{{\rm mem},i})+N_{\rm f,5D}$ . $P({\rm field})$ and $P({\rm cluster})$ are then calculated as $N_{\rm field}/(N_{\rm field}+N_{\rm cluster})$ and $N_{\rm cluster}/(N_{\rm field}+N_{\rm cluster})$ , respectively. We use the corresponding fractions of the total sample as the priors in the Bayesian contamination calculation. We construct the control-field sample by selecting stars within the smallest region in RA, Dec, proper motion, and parallax space that encompasses the cluster members. For stars with available radial velocities, the models incorporate the full 6D kinematic information together with $G$ magnitude and $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ ; for stars without radial velocities, we use the corresponding 5D astrometric information. The resulting contamination probabilities are shown in Figure 7. Including radial velocities where available does not substantially change the contamination estimates or the resulting interpretation of the long-period stars. Five of the ten long-period Hyades stars have relatively high $P_{\rm field}$ ( $>$ 0.01), indicating that they could be field contamination. This removes all stars with $P_{\rm rot}$ $>$ 80 days. In contrast, the five long-period Praesepe stars and rest of the five Hyades stars have low $P_{\rm field}$ , providing stronger evidence that they are genuine cluster members. Notably, several of these likely cluster members have rotation periods of $\sim 60$ –70 days.

We also cross-matched the field sample with similar 5D kinematics to the clusters against the field rotation-period catalog described in section II. We find that 17% and 3% of the field stars around the Hyades and Praesepe, respectively, have detected rotation periods. Using these samples, we performed a Monte Carlo analysis to quantify the expected contribution of field contamination to the observed slow-rotator population. We first constructed mock cluster CMDs from the corresponding field samples by selecting, for each cluster star, a random star from the 50 closest field stars in $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ and Gaia $G$ magnitude. We then calculated the fraction of slow rotators ( $P_{\rm rot}>35$ days) in each mock cluster sample, noting that most field stars do not have measured rotation periods. We repeated this procedure 5000 times to obtain the distribution of slow-rotator fractions expected from field contamination. Finally, we compared this distribution with the membership-probability-weighted slow-rotator fraction measured in the actual cluster sample. None of the 5000 mock Praesepe samples contains a slow rotator, indicating that the observed Praesepe slow-rotator population cannot be reproduced by the field sample in our Monte Carlo realizations. For the Hyades, the observed slow-rotator fraction lies $5.6\sigma$ above the distribution expected from field contamination. This provides strong evidence that the observed slow-rotator population is an intrinsic property of the clusters rather than a result of field-star contamination.

We also examine the period distribution in different $M_{G}$ bins for different membership probability thresholds, assessing whether it provides a reliable criterion for identifying cluster members. We then compare the fraction of stars with $P_{\rm rot}$ $>35$ days as a function of $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ between the field and cluster samples to determine whether the field population alone can explain the observed population of slow rotators.

In addition, we compare the fraction of long-period rotators as a function of photometric temperature between field stars and the two clusters. As a thought experiment, if the peak is associated with the FC boundary, this raises the possibility that the location and width of the slow-rotator peak could provide a new way to probe the metallicity distribution of a stellar population. Since the field sample spans a broader range of metallicities, it is also plausible that its slow-rotator peak is broader than those of the clusters. In addition, a transition in the temperature–radius relation has been observed around 3200–3300 K [68], corresponding to a mass of approximately $0.2,M_{\odot}$ , which may also be associated with the FC boundary and coincides with the location of the peaks in the Hyades and Praesepe.

### III.3 Period Distribution

After establishing that field-star contamination is unlikely to fully explain the long-period population, in this section, we first examine the rotation periods in the context of the CMD, and then investigate the rotation-period distribution as a function of color and effective temperature by combining our measurements with those from the literature.

It is clear that the stars with measured rotation periods lie along a tight sequence, consistent with expectations for a coeval stellar population. In addition, stars identified as potential binaries are predominantly overluminous relative to the main sequence, as expected for unresolved multiple systems. The slowly rotating stars preferentially lie toward the hotter edge of the sequence, consistent with their weaker magnetic activity associated with their rotation and, consequently, reduced radius inflation. This could indicate that the transition from partially to fully convective interiors is associated with a change in the efficiency of magnetic braking, potentially allowing stars near this transition to reach unusually long rotation periods [9, e.g.,].

### III.4 The activity-rotation relation

Stellar activity is known to be correlated with a star’s rotation period through the Ro–activity relation. The behavior of the Ro–activity relation across the fully convective boundary is therefore particularly relevant for understanding the long rotation periods identified in our sample. If the slowly rotating fully convective stars have unusually large Rossby numbers, their weak magnetic activity could indicate a reduced efficiency of angular-momentum loss. Conversely, if these stars remain magnetically active despite their long rotation periods, this would suggest that the standard Ro–activity relation does not adequately describe the magnetic behavior of fully convective stars. We therefore compare the activity of our cluster stars with their rotation periods to investigate whether the slowly rotating stars exhibit anomalous magnetic activity near and beyond the fully convective boundary.

The sample size is small, and the scatter in the $R_{\rm var}$ –Ro relation is known to be large [75, e.g.,]; nevertheless, an activity plateau is still apparent for Ro $\lesssim 0.1$ , indicating the saturated regime. At Ro $\gtrsim 0.1$ , $R_{\rm var}$ decreases with increasing Ro, consistent with the unsaturated regime. In the unsaturated regime, FC stars appear to lie systematically above PC stars, consistent with the recent 15 pc M-dwarf study showing that the photometric amplitudes of fully convective M dwarfs do not depend strongly on rotation [Pass2023]. This is also consistent with studies suggesting differences in magnetic-field topology and angular-momentum loss between FC and PC stars [49, 76, e.g.,]. However, this appears to be in tension with previous studies of magnetic activity indicators, such as X-ray and H $\alpha$ emission, which generally find similar activity–Ro relations for PC and FC stars [92, 39, 59, e.g.,]. It is worth noting that previous studies of magnetic activity in the Praesepe and Hyades have been largely limited to the saturated regime as the longest measured rotation periods are $\sim 30$ days, corresponding to $Ro\sim 0.2$ for a 3500 K star. Thus, the absence of a clear difference between FC and PC stars in these studies does not necessarily rule out a difference in the unsaturated regime, as the FC stars in these young clusters provide limited leverage on the activity–Ro relation beyond the saturation threshold. Given the large intrinsic scatter in the activity–Ro relation and the uncertain transition between the saturated and unsaturated regimes at $Ro\sim 0.1$ , the behavior of FC stars in the unsaturated regime remains difficult to constrain. Furthermore, field-star samples of FC stars are typically small and exhibit substantial non-detections or scatter at large Ro [89, 57, e.g.,]. However, our sample is similarly limited in size and exhibits considerable scatter, and we therefore refrain from drawing strong conclusions about the difference between FC and PC stars in the unsaturated regime.

More generally, the choice of rotational variable may itself affect the apparent form of activity–rotation relations. Stassun and Kounkel [80] found that the empirical relation between X-ray activity and rotation in young stars becomes substantially simpler when rotation is expressed in terms of stellar angular momentum rather than $P_{\rm rot}$ alone. This raises the possibility that some of the apparent mass dependence, and perhaps some of the structure across the FC boundary, in period- or Rossby-based activity relations reflects the strong mass dependence of stellar structure. A future comparison of the present activity measurements directly against stellar angular momentum could therefore provide a complementary test of whether FC and PC stars obey intrinsically different activity–rotation relations.
